title: What happens when we add neighbouring even numbers?
description: The even numbers two, four, six, eight and ten are added in neighbouring pairs, and the sums are lined up to see how they change. Each sum is four more than the one before. Keeko doubts this and says the sums go up by two, like the even numbers.
teaching_notes: One idea: both numbers of a pair go up by two, so the sum of the pair goes up by four. Watch for students who think the sums go up by two because the numbers do.

source: Add each pair of neighbouring even numbers: 2 and 4, 4 and 6
video_script.why: The child makes a new sequence by adding neighbouring terms of a sequence from the book, and sees how that new sequence changes.
video_script.substitution: The book adds neighbouring triangular numbers; here the even numbers from the book are used.
video_script.anchor: the even numbers from the book, with a bracket round each neighbouring pair
video_script.wrong_answer: the sums go up by two each time
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says the sums go up by two each time, like the even numbers. The first two sums are six and ten, which are four apart, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The sums are six, ten, fourteen and eighteen, going up by four each time
maths_rules: each pair has both numbers 2 more than the pair before, so the sum is 2 + 2 = 4 more
video_script.design: The even numbers sit in a row. A bracket slides along them pair by pair, and each sum drops below its pair. The sums are then compared.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the sums go up by two each time, like the even numbers.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>But the first two sums are six and ten, which are four apart.
<bookmark mark='why'/>Both numbers in a pair go up by two. Their sum goes up by two and two together.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>That is four.
